title: AI's third era is the persistent co-worker, and the product cycle is only three months
dek: OpenAI product lead Tara Seshan argues that AI products are moving from chat to agents to persistent co-workers, that you have to build for the model's capabilities two to three months out, and that the future of work is steering rather than rowing — and that writing as thinking should never be automated.
why: Front-line product management experience, with practical judgments on model cycles, writing trade-offs and product marketing fit — directly useful to teams building AI products.
who: AI product managers, founders, investors, and engineers who want to know what the future of work looks like.
skip: You can skip the craftsmanship discussion at 42:22; it doesn't affect the main thread.

points.h: Build products for the model's capabilities two to three months out
points.body: Tara divides the evolution of AI products into three eras: the first era is chat, the second is collaborating with agents, and the third, coming soon, is working alongside a persistent co-worker who can get things done with you. She stresses that when building a product you should base it neither on the current model's capabilities nor on a prediction of where the model will be a year from now, but on the model's capabilities two to three months out, because both extremes fail.

points.h: The future of work is steering, not rowing
points.body: Tara believes the future of work will be more about "steering" than "rowing": agents do the execution, humans set the direction. The level of abstraction at which you steer will keep rising, but ultimately humans still have to make opinionated decisions. She stresses that even as the steering layer rises, human judgment and accountability at key junctures remain irreplaceable — which is both the responsibility and the value.

points.h: The end state of a product is that users don't have to choose tools
points.body: Tara explains that ChatGPT's "work mode" is Codex underneath, but with a different UI. The product's north star is to let users not have to choose, with the system automatically picking the right tool for the task. She stresses that "done beats perfect" — get it into users' hands first, then fix it based on feedback; fast iteration matters more than polish, and, she says, "this is the worst the model has ever been."

points.h: Codex didn't change; what changed is users' perception
points.body: The host observes that the tenor of discussion about Claude Code and Codex on Twitter has shifted over the past few months, with more people leaning toward Codex. Tara responds that the Codex team has always stayed user-oriented and iterated fast, and that how it operates internally hasn't changed — the market and users have just gradually come to see it. She thinks the change isn't in the team but in users' perception.

points.h: The part of writing that is thinking should never be automated
points.body: Tara distinguishes "writing as thinking" from "writing as reporting." She never automates the former, because it is the key to organizing her thoughts; the latter she hands entirely to the model. She recommends writing a doc to 70% and then getting feedback, rather than chasing perfection. At OpenAI she still writes a lot of docs, but mainly for herself, because long documents are no longer a signal of depth of thought.

points.h: Before product-market fit, there is product marketing fit
points.body: The most important lesson Tara learned at Sutter Hill is that product-market fit matters, of course, but she underestimated "product marketing fit." Before you build the product, you should already be sharpening the narrative and positioning through a lot of selling. She believes excellent product marketing work can decide a company's success or failure, and says Mike Speiser is unmatched at it.

terms.def: An AI agent that works with you over the long term and proactively completes tasks, as distinct from one-off chats or short-lived agents.
The degree to which a product's narrative and positioning match the needs of a market segment, with the emphasis on sharpening positioning through selling early on.
